PASSO 1: Outra diferença: o alemão não u: STEP 1: good news first: German possessives work like English ones — no article before them. "My father" is mein Vater, never der mein Vater. STEP 2: the owner picks the stem (my → mein, his → sein, her → ihr); the thing owned picks the ending (mein Vater, meine Mutter).
O português diz “seu” e “sua” para tudo:: English already gets the owner right: "his father", "her father". German does the same with sein and ihr. The difference: the German possessive also takes an ending that agrees with the thing owned — something English never does. So "his mother" is seine Mutter and "her father" is ihr Vater. And watch the triple meaning of ihr: «ihr» = her / their, «Ihr» (capital) = your (formal), and «ihr» = you all.
«Haben» (ter) é irregular. O objeto dire: «Haben» (to have) is irregular. The direct object of «haben» goes into the accusative. In the masculine singular, «ein» becomes «einen» and «kein» becomes «keinen»; in the feminine, neuter and plural nothing changes: «Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe eine Schwester. Ich habe ein Kind. Ich habe keine Kinder».
em português o objeto direto não muda de: English shows the same idea only in pronouns: "he" sees, but you see "him". German does it with articles too, but only for masculine nouns: «ein Bruder» (the one who is) becomes «einen Bruder» (the one you have) — like he → him.

Os possessivos concordam com a COISA pos: Possessives agree with the THING owned (gender and number), in their ending: «mein Vater», «meine Mutter», «mein Kind», «meine Eltern». They take the same endings as «ein»: no ending for masculine and neuter, -e for feminine and plural. The stem comes from the owner, as in English: «sein» = his (or its), «ihr» = her (and their); «Ihr», capitalized, is the formal "your". Careful: «unser» and «euer» lose the inner -e- before an ending: unsere, eure.
